speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR MEASURE TO AMEND-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion for the unanimous consent of the House. I have sent a copy of this motion to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to give him the opportunity, which I am sure he welcomes, of supporting it in the House.
Action to alleviate the revenue problems of the national capital region and other Canadian municipalities is now past due. Considerable distress has been caused by the failure to update the government's policy on grants in lieu of taxes, particularly in the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton where the decision to send public servants to Hull during the business day has left a large number of taxpaying businesses in serious difficulty. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott):
That the government proceed immediately with the introduction of an act to amend the Municipal Grants Act, and arrange to send the subject matter to the appropriate standing committee, to enable the committee to fully examine the question of grants in lieu of taxes, and hear representatives of interested municipalities.

subsubtopic: RESCISSION OF GRANTS TO PROFITABLE COMPANIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Yesterday the President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) announced a $235 million giveaway at the taxpayers' expense
to large, profitable pulp and paper companies in Canada. This morning Domtar, one of the recipients of this handout, announced the acquisition of Reed Paper Limited, of Toronto. In view of Domtar's profits of $63 million in 1978, an increase of 136 per cent over the previous year, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House strongly urges the government to rescind the policy announced yesterday of providing large, profitable pulp and paper companies with the taxpayers' money, since the industry is simply using these profits to increase their concentration without providing one additional new job in the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO PROTECT VICTIMS OF RAPE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The rape bill, C-52, presented for first reading by the former minister of justice has been abandoned by the present minister. The bill redefined rape for the purpose of ensuring the protection of the victim from cross-examination with reference to past sexual conduct, all of which was requested by all women's organizations in Canada. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling):
That the Minister of Justice produce a new bill assuring the protection of the raped victim from being brutalized by cross-examination and being categorized as a compellable witness by the defence to determine the right to produce such evidence in a voir dire, meaning a trial within a trial, and its admissibility during the main trial to prevent fear tactics against victims reporting the crime in question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of serious and urgent necessity which involves the blatant misuse of public funds and the pursuit of narrow, partisan political motives in allocating funds on a constituency basis under the current Young Canada Works program. An analysis of the allocations made to the 23 constituencies in British Columbia shows that the ridings represented by Liberal members have received 50 per cent of all funds available to the entire province despite the fact that the allocations cannot be related to or reconciled with youth unemployment statistics. That the Minister of Employment and Immigration be required to lay before the House immediately, or at least before any disbursement of the S6 million dollars allocated to British Columbia is made, all documentation and criteria on which the allocations are based and that the minister be instructed to cease forthwith this ridiculous practice of political pork-barrelling.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the stated aversion of the Minister of Fisheries to the construction of even one freezer-trawler by Canadians for the catching of presently underutilized species, while licensing in 1978 some 300 foreign factory ships and some 190 freezer-trawlers within our 200-mile limit, an action which is decreasing the supply of fish for our inshore fishermen, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the minister institute a policy to progressively decrease the number of foreign factory ships and freezer-trawlers within our economic zone for 1979.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STUDY OF SOCIAL AND SOCIO-ECONOMIC EFFECTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the terms of Standing Order 43 on an increasingly urgent matter. Since the establishment and expansion of the number of government-operated lotteries has coincided with a general decrease in charitable donations to private sector volunteer service organizations, and considering that there is evidence that lower and middle income groups are disproportionate buyers of those lottery tickets, I ask leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni):
That this House urge the government to undertake a thorough study of the social and socio-economic effects of the lotteries to determine whether they are becoming a voluntary tax aimed at the poor while crippling the ability of private sector agencies to raise sufficient funds to help the same people.

It has been found in some circumstances by some speakers in certain contexts that certain language has been unparliamentary, and in other cases precisely the same language has been found by other speakers in other contexts and other circumstances to be parliamentary. Therefore, there is not much assistance in the precedents in this regard, except for one or two very clear expressions. For example, wherever it has been used, the word "liar" has never been deemed to be an acceptable expression to be used by anybody. In so far as the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission is concerned, the answer to the above question is as follows:
1. It is the present policy of the CRTC to encourage the carriage of the House of Commons proceedings on cable channels other than the community channel. The reason for this is that the commission has for many years adopted a principle of supporting and encouraging community programming, that is to say programming produced in, and for the local community, through setting aside a dedicated cable channel for this purpose.
Over the years there have been many pressures to use this channel for purposes other than community programming, including such matters as educational programming, programming of a general interest nature but not local in origination, and more recently for the carriage of the parliamentary debates.
Although there is unused time on the community channel in many systems, giving over this time to other programming services would have the effect of gradually eroding the special

purposes for which the community channel was established, namely to be of direct help to local communities.
It is possible to carry portions of the parliamentary debates which relate to local issues and involve members of parliament from the particular local area in the context of locally produced programs. This would be entirely within the present regulations governing the use of the community channel.
It should be emphasized that the commission is not preventing cable licensees from carrying not only the question period but the full proceedings of the House of Commons on the basic cable service. This would of course mean displacing a United States' channel in most cases, a decision which cable licensees are reluctant to make.
Furthermore, the governor in council could issue directions to the commission requiring the establishment of a special dedicated channel on all cable systems on the basic service for the carriage of the House of Commons proceedings in accordance with section 15 of the Broadcasting Act of 1968.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned yesterday evening we were debating Bill C-2, and I had already made some remarks but I had not had the honor nor the advantage of hearing the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) when she spoke because I was not in the House. Having read her comments, I am going to be briefer, because she answered several of the questions I proposed to deal with this afternoon.
Now I am convinced that before the bill was brought forward the minister asked herself whether the cancellation of the federal contribution to the Health Resources Fund might not reduce the level of health care in Canada. She said the following, and I quote:
During those discussions it seemed obvious, I believe, that the decision to anticipate the final date for the expiry of that Canadian legislation which was aimed at the construction, acquisition, renovation and purchase of equipment and buildings for the individual training of health personnel will not create serious problems concerning production and health manpower in Canada or the availability of necessary institutions for that purpose.
I am convinced that there were studies on that subject and that the minister decided to recommend to stop the federal contribution from September 9, 1978. Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I am also convinced that the minister will tell us at one point of the report stage what was the level of contributions paid by the federal government under the provisions of chapter H-4, of the legislation, and how much the national treasury could save by dropping this program. I hope she will tell us too whether the measure contemplated by Bill C-2 is a final decision or whether she may at one point come up with another bill to maintain the past levels of the federal contributions.
This puts an end to my remarks on this matter and I do hope that the passing of this bill will not limit the efficiency of our medical services or be an obstacle to the training of the staff to meet the needs of Canadians in health care.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to spend a few moments commenting on Bill C-2 on the health resources fund. I want to congratulate some of last night's speakers, and in particular my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), who, very ably, spoke on the matters of health problems related to the Indians, the Inuit
February 2, 1979

and the native communities. I will come back to that subject and refer to it a little later in my comments.
First, I want to make some general comments regarding the health resources fund. I am sure, as all hon. members will know, that when this particular program was instituted in 1966 it was done in conjunction with the imminent introduction of the medicare program, and indeed of the hospital diagnostic programs, and it was done so that we would be sure there would be adequate facilities, adequate personnel and adequate research, all of those parameters that are essential and necessary if we are to provide an adequate health delivery system to all Canadians.
It was of some interest that on November 30 of last year, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) made reference to this, and I should like to quote from that particular document. She said the following, at the outset:
With the impending introduction of a medical care program, and anticipated shortages of health manpower to meet program and population requirements for increased health services, the health resources fund was enacted on July 11,
1966, to run for the period 1966-1980.
The provisions of the act were to offer financial assistance to the provinces and territories in the planning, acquisition, construction, renovation and equipping of health training facilities.
There was a good deal of additional information, but I want to quote from page four of that same document where the minister stated the following:
In summary, the health resources fund has now achieved its primary objective of assisting the provinces and territories with the provision of the necessary training facilities to satisfy current and future requirements of health manpower in the major health decisions to meet provincial needs.
One of the difficulties with this bill and the implications and conclusions of the bill is that obviously one has to conclude that the minister is implying that all the problems relating to the delivery of health care to Canadians have been resolved. One must come to that inescapable conclusion. As I indicated a moment ago, I want to return in a moment or two to the specific issue of the desperate health problems affecting the native people in Canada, and to review in a general way some of the problems that exist as they relate to our health delivery service in Canada today because, as I indicated, there is an implication in the bill presented by the minister that when she cuts back and then terminates this program on very short notice, all our problems will have been resolved.
Back in 1973 and 1974 I can recall speaking in this chamber, and at subsequent times since then, about the difficulties we have with the health care delivery system in this country. 1 do not pretend to have adequate time to cover all these aspects, but I thought it might be useful to make reference to some of the deficiencies that exist in our system. I thought that last evening the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would mention some of them. If the minister were truly responsible and had a genuine interest in the health of Canadians, she would have addressed herself to some of these problems rather than terminating a program which, in my view, has been successful in the past.
When I spoke in past instances I tried to look at the health care system from a different perspective. For example, I like to
Health Resources Fund Act
think of the broad category of what I refer to as the organization and management of the health care delivery system. Let me put it in simpler terms, if I can. When I am referring to that particular category, I am talking about all those aspects of our health care system including manpower needs, including the various facilities that are available, whether they are hospitals, nursing homes or paraprofessional individuals, all those areas that are relevant to the delivery of the health care system as it exists in the Canadian context. I think I should point out that this has been the primary preoccupation with respect to health matters across Canada. Certainly this is where the major emphasis and major concern are today.
There is nothing wrong with that approach; it is important and necessary. There may well have to be a different rationalization of that system, but certainly that organization in its broadest context has served us well.
There are many components to this broad category to which 1 referred. Let me indicate briefly two or three problem areas that are unresolved and to which the minister has not addressed herself. I think they are pertinent in the total context of health delivery when one talks about the cutting back of funds resolving all the problems of the delivery of health care. Of course this is a reflection of the attitude of the minister.
There are one or two very brief examples which 1 would like to give in the area of health care organization and management. Let us look for a moment at the whole problem of physician manpower requirements. If you look carefully you will find a major problem in the area, and I have not heard the minister address herself to this problem. I can assure you that in my travels across the country, particularly in the northern parts of Canada, the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and the northern part of Manitoba represented by my good colleague, the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith) I found a discrepancy in terms of the services available and the type of professional individuals who are required to provide the quality care which we would hope for and anticipate from a system that is universal in scope which exists in Canada at present.
Another small area is the various small disciplines in the medical profession itself. I am one of those who has been somewhat concerned in recent years about the disproportionate number of individuals who appear in these various disciplines. For example, we know there was a time when a large number of graduates from our medical schools went into what appeared at that time to be some of the more glamorous specialties. There was a period of time when we appeared to have a lack of general and family practitioners and specialists such as ophthalmologists and psychiatrists. We would see individuals bypassing those specialties which are most important to Canadians and becoming involved in what are considered in many instances to be more glamorous types of specialties.
I cannot avoid commenting on the whole area of physician manpower without making a comment on physicians who are emigrating to the United States, a problem about which I am somewhat concerned. Recently I was talking to my son who is

February 2, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
presently doing some postgraduate work in London at the University of Western Ontario. He was telling me about a skit they had put on at one of the med functions. They had a sweat shirt which had on it "Med '78-United States '79". I think that is a particular omen. If one looks carefully at the figures within the last year or two, one will find a very substantial number of Canadian physicians have moved south of the border.
I should like to refer to two colleagues in my own small community whom I know very well. They were born and raised in the area, all their ties were in the area. When they were both at the peak of their careers in family practice, they moved south of the border to Tennessee. The minister should address herself to this question: why are these very important individuals, many of whom were born in and raised families in the Canadian context, moving south of the border?
The minister would find it of some value if she read a recent document produced by four students at the University of Waterloo. As I recall, these students were involved in computer technology, and perhaps mathematics and physics. They undertook the particular project of writing a thesis on the emigration of doctors from the province of Ontario to the United States. I realize the conventional wisdom is that the vast majority are doing so for economic reasons. I suggest the minister, and indeed all members of the House, should read that particular thesis. The reasons are far more extensive than straight financial ones. I have no intention of going into the details, but in many instances the reasons for this emigration have been red tape and fighting with bureaucracy. I am sorry to say also that a number of them virtually have lost faith in the country and do not see a future under the present government.
As I have discussed in the past, there must be some rationalization of the regionalization of health care. I am convinced the minister has not devoted enough time to looking at extended care facilities, home care, nursing homes, and other areas important to the delivery of quality health care across the country.
Briefly, I should like to refer to environmental health matters. 1 am sure all hon. members are very aware of the so-called conventional environmental health problems, such as the problems of impure air, the quality of drinking water, adequate food processing to ensure the health standards of individuals, and sewage and garbage disposal so that various vectors, insects and animals cannot spread disease. We are all aware of those problems, but it is only the surface of significant environmental health problems across the country. Without going into a lot of detail, I should like to refer to some other examples.
The issue of mercury poisoning was raised in the House of Commons approximately three years ago. The problem of mercury poisoning is a very important one, particularly as it relates to White Dogs, Grassy Narrows and the Cree in northern Quebec. Also there are the problems of PCBs, arsenic

poisoning, cadmium poisoning, and lead poisoning. I do not know how many members are aware of the problem with cadmium poisoning, but one governmental departmental official indicated that an Inuit working at Nanasivik Mines in the Northwest Territories had cadmium levels far above those acceptable. I am sure members are aware that cadmium is a very toxic agent. It can be damaging to the liver, the gastrointestinal tract and the nervous system. Also I am sure members are aware of the fact that lead is an environmental problem.
There are many other examples of what I consider to be environmental problems, but if one looks objectively at this area one will find that in most instances the average individual has little control over them. In many instances it is necessary to have government intervention from time to time. We have witnessed such intervention in many instances, yet I am not sure the government accepts or recognizes this very fundamental principle. If one reviews the literature dealing with environmental health problems, one will realize that we have very little knowledge in this area. Of course that implies that more research and development are required.
The minister suggested cutting back health funds, with the implication that there are no problems in the delivery of health care, and virtually ignored the problems of environmental health. Presumably the funds which are being saved could go to far greater use. For example, there is the entire problem of urbanization and the trend toward it in the last 20 years. There are a great number of socioeconomic health problems associated with urbanization, most importantly the noise factor. Indeed the urbanization phenomena have been evident in our native communities, particularly those in the far north which have experienced a sudden inter-relationship of southern Canadians with Inuit or other natives who have not had such exposure in the past. Various health problems exist in that context. In many respects they are environmental health problems, problems which virtually have been ignored by the government.
Another area I should like to deal with is that of human biology. Approximately one week ago I talked extensively about this matter in the House of Commons, particularly in terms of the value of basic medical research. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not in her seat at the moment. Hopefully she recognizes that there is some importance in long-term planning. I feel that she implied it in her announcements in December, but I object to the formula she applied. Without going into the details of the formula, if one analyses it carefully one will find the index used by the minister is tied to various aspects and products in the normal consumer society, items unrelated to those utilized by the science and technology field.
We all recognize inflation in cost has been far greater in that particular field than the other items included in the index which the minister felt were appropriate to use for the formula. In all sincerity I say to the government and the minister that that particular formula should be reassessed. Even though there appears to be an understanding of the importance of long-term commitments, I am sure the minister and the gov-
February 2, 1979

ernment will find a further and very definite erosion in terms of the moneys required for adequate medical research across the country.
The last item is what I have referred to as lifestyle health. I think this is emerging as one of the significant problems and one that has, unfortunately, received little attention from this government. Let me give two or three examples to try to explain what I mean by lifestyle health. This means all aspects of activities over which individuals can exert decision and control. It has been calculated that if we had the facilities, the scientific know-how today, virtually to eliminate every form of cancer known to us, we would increase the life expectancy of Canadians by two to three years.
Then there is the problem of obesity. It has been calculated that if every Canadian were to reduce their weight to what is normal, their life expectancy would be increased by six to seven years. That is what I mean by lifestyle health. That is a classic example.
I do not want to get into figures but I should like to list some of the problem areas. One figure which has impressed me over the years refers to what I call potential years of life loss. If we assume that all Canadians should live to an average age of 70 and that someone dies at age 30, what we are saying is that that individual lost 40 years of potential life. If we keep that formula in mind then it is very interesting to look at the list of the causes of loss of potential years of life.
I am not going to quote the figures, but I should like to read a list of causes. At the top of the list comes motor vehicle accidents. The potential years of life lost due to this cause are far greater than in any other category. Next comes ischemic heart disease, then other accidents, followed by respiratory disease and lung cancer, then suicide; cancer of the breast, uterus and ovary; cerebral vascular disease; gastro-intestinal cancer; leukemia and cirrhosis of the liver.
I could go on, but I want to consider another document now to point out what I consider as potential preventable causes in terms of potential years of life loss. I think this is significant in that it has been ignored by this government. The list is as follows: Motor accidents, ischemic heart disease, other accidents, respiratory disease and lung cancer, suicide, and cirrhosis of the liver. I simply say that these are potentially preventable diseases that would fit into the category of lifestyle health.
One of the major problems with this bill as I see it is that the minister has not addressed, nor have individuals in this House, the very fundamental issue of the effectiveness of the universal program that was introduced for hospital diagnostic services and for the medicare program.
Recent studies carried out in Nova Scotia, Saskatchewan and Quebec and by the Ontario Economic Council subcommittee on health revealed a number of very interesting facts. 1 should like to refer to one which substantiates the point that I am trying to make. The studies show that about 65 per cent of the population of Ontario seeks national health care in any one
Health Resources Fund Act
year. Strong evidence is emerging-and this is important- that the 35 per cent not using services represents the poor and impoverished. These were the very groups that precipitated universality and government intervention. The reasons for this pattern do not entirely seem clear but may relate to the sociological variable of how these groups see sickness and the immediate geographical availability of physician manpower.
I think that is an extremely important observation. When the universal health care assistance programs were defined, whether hospital diagnostic services or medicare, we were saying that we wanted a program that would make available to all Canadians, irrespective of background, quality health care. In all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, I say that we have not accomplished that. In the cities of Canada there is still evidence of rickets and other disease. I am convinced that the group of individuals that the universal programs were designed to reach and to assist has not benefited.
That is the significant point, Mr. Speaker. Nowhere is that more obvious then in the Indian and Inuit community of this country. Last night the hon. member for Wetaskiwin referred to this problem in Alberta and gave some very revealing figures which indicated how serious it is.
I have learned that statistics are very boring, Mr. Speaker, but all the same I should like to refer to a document entitled "Mortality among the registered Indian population" by Pauline Jull of the departmental statistics division of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which puts into perspective the seriousness of the health problem in the native community. The report concludes as follows:
In summary, we conclude that our findings show that mortality is indeed higher among the registered Indian population than among the Canadian population. If mortality differentials can be used to reflect and compare the social and economic conditions of various segments of the Canadian population, then the results just presented in this analysis would tend to indicate that the registered Indian population is substantially disadvantaged compared to the Canadian population as a whole. In light of this fact, it would appear that if the mortality of our native peoples is to be reduced, not only will better access to health facilities have to be provided but significant improvement in their standard of living will have to occur as well.
If I had the time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out some inconsistencies which occur between the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Fisheries and the Environment. It is like musical chairs, Mr. Speaker. There is no corollation, and this was demonstrated in the debate on mercury poisoning which took place on an opposition day.
I should like to give a couple of examples of this mortality because I think it is important that hon. members understand its significance. Six categories of causes of death are listed in this report. The first is infective and parasitic diseases. The age-standardized death rate for the Indian population is 26.77 while the rate for the rest of the Canadian population is 4.98. AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.
Mr. T. Gf*Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands): Mr. Speaker, this legislation amending the Health Resources Fund Act was debated at some length on second reading and was given a very thorough examination, as I understand it, before the standing committee. It would, therefore, seem that there is little value in extended debate on third reading, because it is perfectly clear that the government intends to use its very large majority to push this legislation through parliament.
I venture to participate in the debate, however, not only because of the impact of the legislation itself, but because of the attitude of mind which it reveals, the emphasis which it gives to certain aspects of our national life, and the disjointed scale of social values which I believe are displayed in the legislation.
We should understand that this legislation comes before the House largely as a result of the announcement which was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on national television on August 1. Prior to this the Prime Minister had attended an economic conference; he had sailed on the Baltic with Chancellor Schmidt of West Germany, he had had a holiday in Morocco, and then returned to Canada to effect a complete reversal of the government's fiscal policies. Up until that time he, and particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), had been telling the Canadian people that what was needed was an increase in the effective economic demand. Therefore the Canadian people should save less and spend more. But on August 1 the Prime Minister announced to the Canadian people that the government would embark on a program of restraint.
His first statement was to the effect that they would cut $ 1 billion from the estimates. Later this figure was raised to $2 billion which it was hoped would be passed by the Parliament of Canada. It is significant to note that the cabinet was called together ten days later to hear what the cuts in the estimates were going to be. This makes me wonder what has happened to cabinet responsibility and solidarity.
One of the long-standing traditions of the parliamentary tradition has been that the Prime Minister is primus inter pares, first among equals, that the decisions that are made are not those of the Prime Minister but of the cabinet, and the cabinet must collectively accept responsibility for those decisions after due process of consultation and discussion. Not so in the matter of restraint! The Prime Minister made the announcement as if he were a president of a country with a presidential system. He then called his cabinet ministers to-

gether who were merely to hear what decisions had been reached by the Prime Minister himself.
In my opinion, that is a very serious indictment of the regard which the government has shown for the parliamentary system. There has been growing concern in this country that we are moving step by step toward some type of presidential system. If ever this was demonstrated, it was on August 1 when the Prime Minister reversed the fiscal policy without even the Minister of Finance or his other ministers having been consulted or made aware of the decision which had been reached by the Prime Minister.
I would suggest that the legislation now before us dealing with the health resources fund has three major defects, and I will deal with them individually.
First, let me point out what this legislation does. This legislation seeks to end the health resources fund which was set up in 1966. It has two years to run and in which there is over $80 million yet to be paid out to the provinces to provide certain essential medical and diagnostic facilities. This was a commitment made in 1966 by the Government of Canada to the provinces of this country as an inducement to sit down with the federal government and work out a medicare program. The provinces came in, some reluctantly, not because they were unwilling to deal with the health problems of the nation but because some of these provinces had very limited financial resources. They knew that the moment they had a medicare program, their research, medical and hospital facilities would not be able to cope with the magnitude of the demand for medical and diagnostic services. Their concern was allayed by the fact that the federal government said that they had no need to worry about that problem.
The federal government said that they were setting up a $500 million fund which would be paid out on the basis of need and as provinces proceeded to improve their health care facilities. The provinces came in on that understanding. This was a contract. This was an obligation entered into by the federal government in return for the provincial governments agreeing to enter into a program which they knew would be extremely expensive and represent a great drain on their financial resources. Now, without any warning and without any consultation, the federal government announces in this legislation that the health resources fund is to be closed, that no more money will be paid out after any commitments made have been dealt with, and that same fund with some $80 million in it, which really belongs to the provincial governments, will be closed. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) put this matter very clearly at page 1520 of Hansard for November 27, 1978, when she said:
Why put an end to a good fund two years before its natural end?
The minister answered her question by saying:
The Government of Canada has a difficult decision to make in applying a major, traumatic restraint on its own expenditures.
It not only had a difficult decision to make but it had to decide whether or not it would break faith with the provincial governments on whose behalf this fund was established. It had
February 2, 1979

to decide whether it was more important to cut some other items in its budget, to clean out some of the waste and extravagance demonstrated amply in the Auditor General's report year after year, or whether instead this fund would be completely eliminated. The provinces would then be left holding the baby, with all the responsibility of carrying on their share of a medicare program but without the financial support which had been promised to them.
My second criticism of this legislation is that it assumes the purposes and the objectives of the health care programs have been attained. Of course, they have not. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) said earlier in this debate that the goals for universal health care have not been realized. That statement is true. It is true because we have only covered part of the program to provide the Canadian people with universal health care.
Let me just briefly give an historical summary of the health care program in this country as it applies over the past 30-odd years. As hon. members know, the first hospital insurance and diagnostic services legislation in Canada was passed in the province of Saskatchewan in 1946 and came into effect on January 1, 1947. It was financed entirely from provincial revenues, despite the fact that in 1945 we had been assured at a federal-provincial conference that the federal government was going to come into the program and share the cost on a 50-50 basis.
That hospital insurance and diagnostic services program was financed entirely by the provincial government of Saskatchewan until 1958. During the course of second reading, some members opposite said that hospital insurance in Canada as a whole was introduced by a Liberal government under Prime Minister St. Laurent. Of course that is not correct. I do not attempt to ascribe any suggestion of misleading when I say that. I think these people are just not familiar with the facts.
It is true that in 1956 the Hon. Paul Martin, then minister of health, introduced legislation to provide hospital insurance shared 50-50 between the Government of Canada and the provincial governments. However, it had in it a proviso which said that the federal government would only pay 50 per cent of the cost if a majority of the provinces representing a majority of the population of Canada agreed to enter the program. That was a fairly safe promise to make because everyone knew at that time that the government of Mr. Duplessis of Quebec and the government of Mr. Drew in Ontario had both stated categorically that they would not support a hospital plan. The only two provinces which had hospital insurance plans were Saskatchewan and British Columbia.
It should be to the everlasting credit of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I do not think sufficient credit has been given, that when he took office in 1957 he kept the commitment he had made to the public in the general election of that year to remove that proviso. The result was that in 1958 hospital insurance and diagnostic services became available to any province which wanted to
Health Resources Fund Act
enter into the plan and pay 50 per cent of the costs and accept the other 50 per cent from the Government of Canada. Of course both Saskatchewan and British Columbia immediately became eligible, and the other provinces one by one fell into place.
That only covers hospital insurance. When we come to medical care, the Saskatchewan government introduced medical care legislation in the fall of 1961. As a matter of fact the last piece of legislation which I introduced as premier of that province was the medicare legislation. It came into effect on July 1, 1962. That too was financed entirely by the provincial government out of its own limited resources.
In 1964 the royal commission which had been set up by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, headed by Mr. Justice Emmet Hall, made its report. In my opinion, that was the finest report on comprehensive health insurance that has ever been printed in the English language.

It is to the
everlasting credit of the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson that his government brought down legislation in 1967 to implement a national medicare program shared by the federal and provincial governments. It came into effect on July 1, 1968.
I enumerate this because those of us interested in this field and those who pioneered this field, and I am not talking so much about politicians but doctors, hospital administrators and sociologists interested in the wider scope of the health program, all reminded the public from time to time that comprehensive medical care would come in two phases.
Phase one was the task of removing the financial barrier between those who render health services and those who receive health services. That is an important phase. As long as that barrier was there, there were people who could not get health services. No matter how deserving or how desperate their circumstances, they could not get those services. Therefore health service had a price tag. It was important to remove that barrier.
At the same time it was pointed out to the people of Canada that removing the financial barrier was only a part of the program. The much more difficult part of a health care program was to reorganize and change the entire delivery system. It had to move from a program which emphasized curative medicine over to a system which emphasized preventive medicine, recognizing that the most important thing is to keep people well rather than merely patching them up after they have become desperately ill.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent made an excellent summary of what is entailed in that regard, such as periodic check-ups for health care, watching people's weight, X-rays, blood tests, urinalysis, checking heart conditions. He also referred to prescribing a proper diet, taking proper preventive measures and sometimes preventive surgery, saving people pain and suffering later on and also saving great amounts of money.

instead of recognizing this to be the case, ministers opposite come before the House and ask us to vote to cancel a health resources fund designed to provide facilities to improve the health of the Canadian people. At the same time, as I have pointed out, they propose to hand out $235 million to an industry which has money running out of its ears. As far as I am concerned, and as far as the New Democratic Party is concerned, we shall not agree to this legislation and what it represents.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) gives a very learned discourse on any subject before the House and is a person to whom we all listen. It was interesting that he should have referred to two phases in the health care system. What he says is, indeed, true. But he forgot to mention the third phase, one which we have not seen so far in Canada but which is presently unfolding in the United Kingdom under the National Health Service. I submit that the third phase is the phase in which one begins to see the breakdown of a health service which is completely under government control.
In the United Kingdom companies wanting to provide adequate health insurance for their employees so that they can receive adequate care so that they can return to work as quickly as possible, now have to get supplementary insurance from private insurers outside the National Health Service. I submit that that third phase will come to Canada unless governments realize that they cannot afford to interfere in the control of health care provisions to the extent they have been. This may be difficult for the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands and some of his colleagues to accept, but if they look at what is happening in Great Britain they will see that that third phase is definitely unfolding there.
Last night a bit of an altercation took place between the minister and the spokesman for my party, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk). speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several philosophies which should be discussed with reference to this bill. We raised these philosophies in committee, and the minister certainly gave us a good hearing and made some interesting comments. I think it is very important that legislators take some cognizance of where we place our priorities in the expenditure of public funds in the health care system. I think we must consider two aspects of funding. We can spend public funds on behalf of individual citizens who need certain health services, and the question is whether the government has a right and a moral responsibility to exact taxes from those people in order to give it back to them in the form of the medical health services they receive.
Another area in the health care system which is very vital and which this government ignores is the area of research. This applies right across the whole scientific community. Individuals citizens have difficulty allocating funds personally to provide for adequate research, and if anybody in society should be responsible for such allocation it should be the federal and provincial governments. If we are coming to a time in our economic history when we are under some pressure, the priority should not be expenditures on behalf of individuals for health care but expenditures on aspects which we as individuals cannot support ourselves. I am referring, of course, to research which requires government action in order to achieve progress.
When I raised this with the minister in the committee, I was pleased with her response. As recorded in Issue No. 7 of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, at page 10, the minister said:
Usually, I would agree with Mr. Halliday's outlook. I think I would favour programs that equip people with facilities, buildings-all these things that permit people to meet and to do their thing.
The minister agreed with me that a high priority for governments should be to do those things for people which the people cannot do for themselves. I was pleased about that.
I believe it was back in 1966 that the government agreed to provide $500 million for the extension and enhancement of training facilities, for health care personnel and for certain aspects of research. Now we come to this year, and we find

February 2, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
that the minister's priorities are different. Although theoretically she agrees with my philosophy that we have to support people in research when they have trouble financing their work, she now turns around and changes her story. I find that very disappointing indeed.
As we look further at the minister's assessment of the situation today, we find that she is cutting back on the funds which her predecessors a number of years ago agreed to provide. We find that she is not making any provision for continuing and upgrading health care facilities. As reported at page 2808 of Hansard for last night, the minister said, and I quote:
As for professional and quasi-professional health groups-
This is the part I want to emphasize.
-we now have in Canada a satisfactory level of personnel with adequate training.
1 do not need to tell the physicians who are in- the House that adequate training is not a lifetime acquisition. It is said that the half-life of a physician's knowledge is five to seven years, and I remind the minister that she should be making provisions for continuing training and the provision of facilities so that this half-life can be extended beyond five to seven years. If physicians do not receive that kind of support, they will be in more difficulty as time goes on, and we are already beginning to see some signs of that.
In this same vein, when the minister was talking to us last night, she had this to say as reported at page 2811 of Hansard:
There will be a need, to a much lesser degree, to maintain and upgrade existing schools and related facilities which in most instances are new or renovated structures.
Again I say that the minister does not seem to realize that it is necessary to keep spending money on the good facilities we already have if we are to maintain them properly.
Last night the minister criticized us for spending so much time discussing medical research. It is paradoxical that she should accuse members of the opposition in that way, and then devote most of her speech to discussing medical research. The minister raved about the contributions her government has been making to medical research over the last few years. The minister would lead the public to believe that the government has made an adequate contribution to the research community. I could quote a number of her comments which would lead people to believe that the government has done a really great job.
It is very interesting that before I heard the minister speak last night, and before she had the nerve to say that the research community is very happy with all the money which is being granted to the Medical Research Council and so forth, yesterday afternoon, I received a letter dated January 29, just Monday of this week, from the executive secretary of the science policy committee of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies. This federation is a very learned body. Its members are very knowledgeable about research. It is too bad the minister did not consult this group before making comments about the adequacy of her support for research. This

letter was not solicited by me. As far as I know I have never been in touch with Dr. John Kucharczyk, who sent this letter to me.
I will not read the entire letter because of its length, but he points out some of the flaws in the minister's argument and the mechanisms upon which the minister based the funding proposals for the Medical Research Council and medical research in general. The plans over a five-year period are that funding for medical research will be based upon the implicit price index of the gross national expenditure. In short terms, it is condensed to IPI-GNE. In coming to a formula, that is modified by the CPI and the GNP minus 1 per cent. It is a rather complicated formula, but the interesting thing is the net effect of it upon medical research. Dr. Kucharczyk obviously is a researcher who is quite capable of bringing out the inherent fallacies in the program for medical research laid down by the minister. At page two of his letter dated January 29, 1979, Dr. Kucharczyk said the following:
Table 1 shows that from 1969-70 to 1978-79 the IPI-GNE underestimated scientific inflation-measured by the Science Expenditures Price Index or SEPI-by a total of 34.2 index points or $16.2 million.
In a budget of approximately $62 million to $63 million annually, I suggest that is a significant underestimate on behalf of medical research.
He continued as follows:
Yet it is precisely this index, the IPI-GNE, that the government intends to use on its new five-year funding formula for MRC announced by Mme Begin on December 1.
Obviously it is disappointing to the medical community, particularly the biological research community, to see the minister, who probably did not have adequate research staff, develop an incomplete and inadequate formula. In order to summarize the feelings of the Canadian Federation of Biological Societies concerning the minister's plans for the future, the closing paragraph of the doctor's letter reads as follows:
In short, our calculations do not support the minister's conclusion that the five-year plan is "A major step ... toward the achievement of greater stability in the federal government's support for biomedical research". The proposed formula neither reflects the true level of scientific inflation nor will it allow health research activities in Canada to expand at a rate commensurate with the growth rate of the economy as a whole.
That is a rather terrible indictment of the minister's plans for medical research. There are more data and several more tables containing information which was gathered by Statistics Canada and the Department of Finance. The figures were developed on behalf of the then minister of science and technology. This information is available if the Minister of National Health and Welfare wants to look at it. I hope the minister will revise her formula to support medical research in a manner satisfactory to the Canadian research community.
Another area I should like to touch on deals with the manner in which the minister brought forth the changes in Bill C-2. As the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands mentioned today, and as the hon. member for Athabasca mentioned last night, the minister made no effort to consult
February 2, 1979

the provinces prior to the institution of this drastic $84 million cut. Often we have seen this type of action occur, particularly respecting the social service programs of the government. If the government wants to be re-elected, it promises Canadians something they want very much-extra money in their pockets. This could be accomplished by promising increased benefits in health care, unemployment insurance or other programs. Usually a government is re-elected if it makes promises to the people.
In this particular instance, the government involved the provinces but gave them no choice. They were forced to agree with the plan, and the government went along with it for a given number of years. A couple of years before the plan was completed the government decided to cut off the provinces, medical research and medical schools across the country. Canadians are becoming wise to this type of action. If the government attempts to bribe people because of the upcoming election, this time I do not think it will be successful.
I should like to refer to what the minister gave as reasons for the cut. Earlier this week the minister was confused when she attempted to answer my question regarding the distribution and submission of T4A tax forms for old age pensions. I am glad the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) is in the House today, as he is very involved in this matter. He was conned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare into allowing changes to his original plans. This is very upsetting to the old age pensioners, but it is inappropriate to discuss it at this time. I wanted only to acknowledge the presence of the Minister of National Revenue. He can be assured we will discuss this matter in the very near future. Members of my party have received letters from old age pensioners all across Canada who were very upset by what the government did with the refunds they should be receiving.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare appeared before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs in order to explain the reasons for Bill C-2. I should like to quote from her four-page introductory comment dated November 30, 1978. The minister made her introductory comments before the committee on December 7, 1978. She said the following:
In summary, the health resources fund has now achieved its primary objective of assisting the provinces and territories with the provision of the necessary training facilities to satisfy current and future requirements of health manpower in the major health disciplines to meet provincial needs.
If one attempts to interpret that statement, the reason for the $84 million cut was that in the minister's opinion we had achieved the main or primary objective of the total fund, and that our needs as far as training facilities were concerned had been satisfied. I suppose those are nice reasons for stopping, but I should like to refer to what the minister said in the House of Commons on November 27, 1978, when she introduced the bill. At that time she was attempting to justify the introduction of Bill C-2, and there was no mention of objectives having been achieved. As reported at pages 1519 and 1520 of Hansard, the minister said:
-despite the reduction due to the fiscal constraints which we think are essential to put the Canadian economy back to full productivity.
Health Resources Fund Act
The minister suggested that the real reason for the introduction of the bill was not because the objectives in health care had been achieved, but because of financial restraints. As reported at pages 1520 and 1521 of Hansard, the minister said:
Regretfully it is to be terminated now because of the difficult conditions in the country.
I cannot put it nearly as well as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, but obviously it was not a cabinet decision; it was the decision of our president or emperor, as he is sometimes referred to. Suddenly we required cuts in our national expenditures, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare was told to make these cuts. The minister used the economy as the reason for depriving our health institutions of $84 million. I do not know how the minister can explain this contradiction. Of course, we are becoming accustomed to contradictions; the list is as long as my arm; nothing is new.
When one considers the problems associated with research, I think one has to mention also that the minister has failed to recognize that we must have long-range planning in the research community. I give her credit for recognizing this to the extent that the Medical Research Council will now be able to move ahead five years in its planning, but by promising $500 million a number of years ago and taking it away before that fund has reached its maturity, she is denying that planning function to our medical schools and to the research community, and she is taking away any opportunity they had to plan ahead.
I do not want to pursue this subject much longer, but there are two things I should like to speak to very briefly, and one is medical manpower. I raise this issue purely because the minister chose to raise it in her speech last night. We discussed this matter in committee when we considered Bill C-2 there. 1 asked the minister whether she had any true understanding of what the actual manpower status is in Canada. She had one of her experts from the department with her in the committee that day to whom she referred the question, namely Dr. Law. The interesting thing is that the department has ideas about the physician population ratio and we were quoted a bunch of figures by the minister last night, but if you ask the minister simply how many practising physicians we have in Canada, she cannot tell us. That is how absurd and how inadequate research is in this country in relation to medical manpower; she cannot tell us how many practising specialists or practising family physicians there are in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: How many are there?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is the kind of research job the Department of National Health and Welfare should be doing, but they refuse to do it, they refuse to accept that responsibility. They come out with glib figures which look good in the papers and which make it appear as though we had many practising physicians here, but included in those figures are people like

February 2, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
the nine of us here in the House of Commons, most of whom are not practising medicine at all, or to a limited extent. All across the country, with increasing bureaucracy, we have more and more professionals working outside the area of delivery of health care, working in some type of administrative capacity with health insurance companies or in various government bureaucracies, yet the minister says that because they are licensed physicians they should be included in the physician population ratio. I have been bugging the minister, as I have her predecessor, to give us some accurate figures, but they cannot do it even after my two or three years of pleading.
I have one final comment that I am prompted to make about one of the remarks of, once again, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) when he spoke about the need for preventive health care. I do not have to be convinced about the need for preventive health care: I am convinced about the inadequacy of governmental efforts to promote preventive medicine, there is no doubt about that. If we have a change of government before too long, we will probably be able to institute some type of incentives in this country which will encourage people to live a lifestyle that will be more conducive to the development of good health. But certainly I want to raise an issue which is a corollary to this very comment regarding preventive medicine that I think needs to be raised here. Not only does it relate to the obligations and responsibilities of the Minister of National Health and Welfare but, I suggest, it relates to the obligations of her sidekick, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo). She has seen fit to cut down the budget of her department by some $5 million to $6 million this year. I was disappointed to hear today, for instance, her announcement of a gift or a grant or some such thing of about $5 million to three cities in Canada for the promotion of professional sport to NHL level. I am a follower of professional sport in Canada. As a matter of fact, I hope to see the Toronto Maple Leafs and Montreal Canadiens play tomorrow night. I have a lot of respect for our professional teams in Canada. There is a real need for them and I think they serve a real purpose. But when I look at the title of the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, I see in it very little about professional sport. I wonder where she found that $15 million to hand out to the three cities, much as I think they might deserve to have better arenas, and I am sure that to some extent the money will be used by amateur sport as well. The point I want to make is that if she has that kind of money for professional sport, which is by and large self-supporting in Canada, I wonder why she cannot find some money for fitness, recreation and amateur sport which has a real bearing on the health of Canadians. If we want to talk about the need for preventive medicine here, we should take a serious look at the amount of money that is being spent in this country on amateur sport and on fitness and at the same time be mindful of the fact that the federal government spends about $400 per person per year on health care. At this year's rate we spend about $1.25 per person per year on fitness and amateur sport, most of which does not sink down to the level of the commu-

nity at which we can do something for the general health of people in Canada by providing them with an opportunity to become more involved in various types of fitness activities and of amateur sport.
I suggest that if we are going to look at the need for cutting back on $84 million in our health resources fund, the minister might well have used that money in another way. If she thinks we have reached the ultimate in our medical plant facilities, in our institutions and in our research, she might well have considered handing over some of that money to her colleague, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, who, I am sure, could have found a way to improve amateur sport with that money and to upgrade the fitness level across the country, thereby doing something worth while for Canadians.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you would understand, after having heard the comments of various members of the opposition- unfortunately we have heard nothing from the government side-our reluctance to support the minister in this third reading debate on Bill C-2.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to participate in this debate together with the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), who has just spoken, and who was preceded by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) who led off the debate for us. I understand I will be followed by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) who I know will make a contribution to this debate. Moreover, it is a great honour for me to participate in this debate with the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Island (Mr. Douglas) and to be in the House with him during this debate, knowing of his great contribution and pioneering effort in this whole area in the province of Saskatchewan, although he would be the first one to admit that some details of it might not have been to his liking. But in general, members on both sides of the House recognize the great contribution he has made in health care in Saskatchewan and also the contribution he made to the debate this afternoon.
It is absolutely incredible to me that in a debate as important as this one on health resources not one member on the government side has addressed himself to this problem today.
We know where their priorities are today. I have known for years where the Liberal priorities have been because they abandoned true Liberal principles years ago. It is no surprise to me that during the so-called restraint period-and previous speakers have already alluded to this-in a week when the federal government can find millions and millions of dollars to aid the paper industry in this country, an industry which has shown fantastic profits, the government is cutting the health resources fund. What in the name of God are they doing? They are curtailing the health resources fund in the same week they found millions of dollars for the paper industry which is making millions of dollars in profit. Where in the name of God are the old Liberal priorities? I will speak to that point later.
There is a lot of yelling across the way, Mr. Speaker. If hon. members opposite have prepared speeches they should get up and deliver them, but I do not suppose they have. No member
February 2, 1979

of the government will speak in the debate this afternoon because they cannot defend the indefensible-either that or they have been muzzled.
A few months ago budgetary cuts were announced, Mr. Speaker. The only reason for them was that this government has so mismanaged the economy that they have given this country the worst economic management since confederation. Who has suffered because of this? With the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the hon. member for Athabasca, and other members of this party's social policy committee, I knew many months ago on whose back the government's restraint program would be carried. Indeed we have proof positive of it. The low income Canadian will carry the load. The first cut was in the wheat subsidy, which of course affected the price of bread and we know how important that is to people on low incomes. Next came the powdered milk subsidy, then family allowances and significant aspects of low income housing. Now, believe it or not, the health resources fund is the victim.
I have to repeat myself, Mr. Speaker, in saying that they are doing this in the same week that they seem to be able to find millions of dollars for business. Is this the Liberal policy of Mackenzie King; of Lester Pearson?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

speechtext: I knew I would hit a nerve somewhere.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The hon. member has hit a nerve. Does the just society fight inflation on the backs of the poor and nobody else?
I am not a socialist, Mr. Speaker but I agree with many of my friends in the New Democratic Party. If there is one thing that governments must do it is care for people who are sometimes getting shafted. Why cannot this government bring in a restraint program that is more imaginative than one that is waged on the backs of those who cannot defend themselves.
The hon. member for Oxford who has just spoken and was so articulate said time and time again in committee that the minister claimed this health resources fund was being terminated because it had already fulfilled its usefulness. As he so ably put it, the minister subsequently said she really had to do that because of budgetary restraints imposed from on high. I happen to know that this fund was cut without her knowledge. That is why she is not here today to defend this bill. It was cut by Treasury Board and the Department of Finance, and the minister went right through the roof. Had it been cut with her knowledge and consent she would be here to defend herself today and would have her minions here to defend her, but she as been muzzled.
The minister said she had consulted the provinces, Mr. Speaker, and that they were quite happy-that the fund had fulfilled its usefulness. However, I made a long distance
Health Resources Fund Act
telephone call to each of the ten provinces to find out the facts. This fund was cut without consent from the provinces. Not one provincial minister of health said that the fund had fulfilled its usefulness. I wonder if the minister could come into this House this afternoon or next week and name one provincial minister who told her or her officials that the fund had fulfilled its usefulness.
There is only one reason for the fund being cut, Mr. Speaker. This government has so mismanaged the economy it has had to make cuts in many fields. The cut in the social field falls on the backs of those Canadians who cannot defend themselves.
I should like to return to the very able speech made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands who has done so much in this field. Let me draw an analogy.
Suppose that tomorrow morning most of us were sitting in a city council and agreed that every body in the city should have free bread and we passed an ordinance or regulation to that effect. The second thing we would do would be to vote income supplementation into people's pockets in order to pay for that bread. I assume that the third thing to be done would be to get in touch with the bakers and tell them to manufacture the bread to meet the demand. What has been done with medical and health care services in Canada, though? Generally speaking, not because of men who have done so well in Saskatchewan, like the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, but because of the stupidity of this government, we have invariably voted income supplementation.
I wish the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) would make a speech-if he is allowed to. Maybe the ministers have been muzzled too.

speechtext: I apologize for interrupting the hon. member, Mr. Speaker. I was not laughing at him, or with him for that matter. I wanted to point out that something like 30 cabinet ministers backed this bill. It was supported at second reading. The minister is not here this afternoon because she has other responsibilities.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Just 30 ministers? What about the others?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
We can imagine what would happen in the city, Mr. Speaker, if after passing an ordinance for free bread and voting income supplementation into people's pockets to buy that bread, it turned out no bread was available. We do not have to imagine the chaos. The population would be starving.
Is it possible the same stupidity is being imposed on our population vis-a-vis medical health care services? We have decreed that every Canadian should have free health care service and we have voted income supplementation into people's pockets for those services, but what about the third step?
Some members who spoke ahead of me talked about preventive medicine. I am aware that the initial concept of the health resources fund was for educational institutions and research. It was meant to be the government's centrepiece, to make sure

February 2, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
that the plan and personnel were in place, if one is to be guided by the speeches made when the fund was set up.
The plan has been imposed on the provinces, and we have been through that debate, Mr. Speaker. It is public policy that the services should be there for everybody in the country, and it is public policy that we are going to vote income supplementation into people's pockets for those services.
Initially the health resources fund was the government's acknowledgement that it had to play a leadership role with the provinces. As the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands have said, it indicated that the plan, the doctors, the institutions, the research facilities-the whole infrastructure, was there.
Today the government has the unmitigated gall to tell us they are cancelling the health resources fund because it has completed stage one of what in my view should be a ten-stage program.
Sometimes it is difficult to determine whether the fund is in the preventive field or the curative field.
Doctors who have already spoken in this debate, such as the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Athabasca, have suggested that it should be an ongoing fund. I challenge the government to come before this House and say that they have had provincial consent to end this fund. That is just not true. The provinces were not consulted, so how could they have ever said that the fund has fulfilled its usefulness?
Originally the fund was set up for research at the university level. Past federal ministers of health and welfare have said time and again that before we can make sense and rationalize either the cost or planning of services we need to rationalize community planning. At the centre of community planning for the delivery of rational and humane medical and health care services is a high degree of emphasis on preventive medicine, home care, community clinics, emergency care research, the facilities and training of paramedical people, extended care centres, chronic care hospitals, and the list goes on. All these things go into the mix of rationalizing a proper organization for community planning, and all these things can be affected directly or indirectly by the extension of the ongoing health resources fund which the minister is cutting by this legislation.
Very often in this House or outside and in committee ministers talk about our supposedly enviable doctor population ratio in Canada as compared to other countries. It may be enviable in a global sense, but the fact is there are still many underserviced areas in this country, whether it be from the lack of primary care by physicians, specialists or paramedical people. This situation could be rectified with a proper exten-tion of the health resources fund. The facts are here for all to see, that this fund is not being cut because the provinces want it or because it has fulfilled its purpose in terms of its phase one objective, but because of the worst economic management this country has seen since confederation. It is being cut by a government that is waging a restraint program on the backs of

the less deserved, less fortunate in this country, and on the backs of the low-income Canadians.
The community hospital should be at the hub of health care and medical services in the community. Medical experts and government planning experts have talked about proper health care service for decades now, but it cannot be realized unless we have public funds allocated for planning and personnel. The only instrument in respect of which the federal authorities had to take initiatives was the very fund which the government is attempting to cut off by this legislation, namely, the health resources fund.
In looking back at the great social initiatives of the St. Laurent government, the Diefenbaker government and the Pearson government-and I am being objective about this-in bygone decades, times before the present, disastrous Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power, we are looking at total annual budgets of $6 billion, I shudder at what we have now. Under the present Prime Minister, who is responsible for devastating our economy, we have seen our total budget go up tenfold from approximately $6 billion to approximately $60 billion. How can they possibly consider themselves a government of a just society? I challenge members opposite, who have voted for increasing the budget by tenfold, session after session to name one major social program they have brought in over the past ten years. They cannot.
This government, while ruining the economy, has not brought in one major social initiative in ten years. The best thing they can do, while passing out millions of dollars to the pulp and paper industry, is to cut out the health resources fund. Where are the great Liberal policies of the past? It is simply "ad hockery" and opportunities which we are seeing from this government. The people of Canada are waiting to turn them out because they are awful.
