At that time I am sure the provinces did not even imagine that the federal government would just pull out, leaving them holding the bag. Is this co-operative federalism? The reason this country is in such a mess today, vis-a-vis unity and federal-provincial relations, is because of actions like this. Is this sort of unilateral pulling-out of programs the kind of federal-provincial consultation and co-operation that the government feels will help the atmosphere of unity in Canada? I do not think so.
Within the past ten days it has been reported by reliable news media that Liberal backbenchers and senior civil servants
February 2, 1979

in the hon. lady's department are saying that her department is in a mess, that she has lost control, and that she has no co-ordinated policies. Members opposite, so-called government supporters and senior civil servants have said that this is nothing but a bunch of "ad hockery" and that the whole department has broken down because of a lack of leadership from the hon. lady. No single item underlines this more than the fact that the government is now asking us to cut back the health resources fund, a fund which has not even completed stage one of its objective. This is not only a very sad day for the country, but for the people of Canada who expect and deserve better, and who will be getting and expecting better in a very few months.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have opposed this bill primarily for two reasons. One reason is the high-handed method the government used to introduce the legislation and its failure to consult with the provinces.
It was a unilateral decision with an announcement to the press, followed five days later by a telex to the provincial health ministers informing them that the fund would be terminated.
The other reason we oppose this bill is because of its detrimental effect on research, by cutting off funds for medical research to an even greater degree than the minister and her predecessors have done over the past decade.
In reviewing the comments made by her on second reading of this bill we find that the minister used the word "dramatic". She said that the government has to take dramatic steps in its restraint program. Whether she realized it or not, she hit the nail on the head when she said that, because those are the only kinds of cuts this government is making in its restraint program-those which are dramatic, and those which evoke or stimulate an outcry of response from the people of Canada. When this kind of dramatic cut is examined carefully, it is revealed as nothing more than political grandstanding. If the government was serious about making cuts it would forget about drama and would look into the Auditor General's report. If ministers took time to study this report they would see the hundreds of pages of suggestions as to where the efficiency of government could be improved and where improved accountability methods could save millions of dollars.
For some strange reason however, these recommendations appear year after year in the Auditor General's report, but each year the circumstances are worse. The government talks about dramatic cuts in spending but seems to avoid those recommendations which would not be so dramatic but which would correct the extravagant waste of millions of dollars.
We in this party have to object to that kind of an approach, an approach by a government that is more concerned with drama than with increasing efficiency and doing something about the excessive waste imposed by its practices and policies.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House are not very impressed with the proposals contained in this bill.
Health Resources Fund Act
As the minister indicated, the health resources fund was established in 1966. The sum of S500 million was set aside to assist provinces in the establishment of health training and research facilities. About 25 per cent of this was to go toward research. So far $416 million has either been committed or already spent. The proposal in this bill as it was originally drawn would allow the federal government to welsh on its commitment to the tune of $84 million. Of that fund, three-quarters was allocated to the construction of facilities for training health professionals, acquiring research equipment and training Canada's brilliant young people for careers in the health field.
Through its austerity the government has decided to chop this fund. The thing that concerns us most is the method used, which again is typical of this government. It did not bother to tell the provinces in advance; it did not bother to consult with the provinces in advance, but just sent a telex about five days after the intention was made public.
In a federal system direct consultation among the responsible governments is essential as a means of ensuring that the goals of all governments are better integrated and more sensitive to the regional and national requirements. For a federal-provincial system of government to operate smoothly, effectively and for the benefit of the people, there must be mutual respect between the provincial and federal governments. There must be a mutual feeling of trust.
The provinces need to trust the federal government. If the federal government makes a commitment, they need to rely on that in order to plan for the future. When the federal government takes the position that commitments are made to be broken, the feeling of trust breaks down. This is why the federal-provincial system has broken down and why unity in this country has been so shattered in the ten years of this regime.
I mentioned earlier that about one-quarter of this fund has been allocated toward medical research. We already know from previous comments made in the House, and indeed from comments made by representatives of the research community both inside and outside of parliament, that funding of medical research has already been seriously eroded. Unsalvageable damage has been done to the research capability of this country. As well, numerous laboratories are idle. Hundreds of research workers have left the country or have left their careers to do other things in order to keep body and soul together. Various technicians have been relieved of their duties and are on the already bulging unemployment rolls. In general, the policies of this government have been creating havoc in research and have caused stagnation in the general attitude toward research. It is nothing short of criminal negligence when funds are cut for health research and facilities in this way. We know that in the long run every human being in this country will be affected during his or her lifetime. This government seems to be saying in this particular instance that the saving of dollars seems to be more important than good health. In my view, and I am sure hon. members will agree, this is certainly false.

Health Resources Fund Act
I want to touch briefly on another matter, Mr. Speaker, and that has to do with the Indian health services guidelines which were implemented only a few weeks ago. The minister indicated that she felt the Indian people as a whole were abusing the health care services that were provided. I want to object to that sort of criticism because I do not see why that particular group of people should be singled out. It is quite easy to see that some people in every group in society are abusing the health care system, to some extent.
Bill C-2 is a cutback bill in the area of health services. The concept of health, if it is to be meaningful, must be viewed in the broadest possible context. The context must encompass the physical and social aspects of a person's well-being. It cannot refer only to the absence of disease. Indian people do not enjoy the state of health enjoyed by other Canadians. This is revealed most dramatically by statistics. The statistics with respect to the health of the Indian people in my province are horrifying. If the minister is concerned about anybody abusing the medical services in this country, she should not single out the weakest group in our society, the Indian people.
In concluding my contribution to this debate, may I commend the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), who is our critic in this area. His participation in this debate has been very worth while, I would also like to commend the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) who outlined the needs of our native people in this country extremely well.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the debate. This is a subject which brings back some personal memories. For some nine years, from 1951-1960, I was employed in the Department of National Health and Welfare as an economist. At that time one of the responsibilities of my section was an analysis of the national health grants and their impact. These grants had been introduced in the period following the second world war by the government of the Rt. Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. As prime minister he intervened in the debate when the legislation establishing the national health grants was introduced. Mr. King said at that time that a fundamental prerequisite to health insurance was the concept of health grants. These grants were to be the instrument of making sure we had the resources both in the capital facilities and in the trained personnel to provide services to the people of Canada on a scale which we hoped to provide. The history of these grants has been described in many different places. The nature of the grants has changed. New grants were introduced. The medical rehabilitation branch was introduced in the late 1950s, for
example. As we look back today we see that the operation of this program has achieved a good deal of its purpose. No doubt we have not achieved all the purposes in mind. The minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in her remarks the other day pointed to the hospital construction grant, a tremendous contribution that has taken place through the encouragement and incentive that was offered. In those days the grant was only $1,000 per bed. That does not sound much in the days of the cheap dollars we have today. At that time it was an incentive to an orderly planning and extension of hospital facilities, and so on down the line. A good deal of the funds were dedicated to medical research. The minister has pointed out that the Medical Research Council is now to be the instrument through which an extended program of grants takes place. National objectives will be undertaken under the very competent advice of professionals named by that council.
What puzzles me when I listen to members opposite is their inconsistency. They tell us they are going to start everything on zero-based budgeting and then prove the need for programs. They are all for reducing deficits, except now and again they want a stimulating deficit. One never quite knows.

The government is saying that after a period of 30 years, since 1948, we are now going to go to a zero-based budgeting approach on health resource funding. It is going to look at health research, the shortage of personnel, justify what is needed and, if specific programs are needed, and if the case is sold, these will be provided by the government and by parliament. They will be provided by this government.
Hon. members opposite say the program is not over, that 30 years is not enough. They say we should keep it going, that we should vote more money and that it is a betrayal of something or other not to keep it going.
The government is saying the time has come to again start from scratch in this area and look at our objectives and our needs, justify the allocation of resources and the relationship to them, and that this is part of an over-all program of restraint.
It is not easy for me in the seat I represent to defend restraint. I represent a seat in the national capital that has a very large number of public servants, many of whom are carrying the burden of the implementation of these policies. We have the difficulty of eliminating the 5,000 positions

I listened to members on the other side talk about the painless method of eliminating 20,000 positions a year for three years. All I know is the people I represent will not buy that. The credibility of the people who try to say they can do all of this painlessly is not going to be accepted either.
If the members of the official opposition mean zero-based budgeting, they have to start practising it somewhere. Mr. Speaker, I was delighted to give way to my hon. friend for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) because it is somewhat disconcerting to be involved in a debate where the government side is shocked into silence. As a matter of fact, you cannot get a debate unless you have give and take across the chamber.
The hon. member for Ottawa West has now stated his case which is in some respects typical of the posture he takes. He does not always agree with government policy. However, in this instance he does agree with the legislation before the House in which the government is asking for third reading passage to meet the needs of the health programs in Canada at the present time.
I wish to say at the outset that this expresses the problem we are confronted with at the present time. We are not able to debate this important piece of legislation from a dispassionate standpoint on the basis of its merit, and there is nothing more important than the health and well-being of Canadians everywhere. Rather, we are debating the matter in an electioneering atmosphere. Obviously the government has told its supporters to be silent because the posture they are taking with regard to this matter is indefensible and they want to get this over with as quickly as possible.
Unfortunately the House and the country have been poised on the brink of this kind of uncertainty for almost a year. Parliament has been turned into a huge election machine. Nothing is done unless it is with the government's eye on the election potential.
The confusion that surrounds this piece of legislation at this time arose from the sudden reversal of policy by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It was a fundamental reversal of policy, a 180 degree change when he spoke over television last August 1 and tried to redirect a government that had been wasteful to the nth degree. It had dragged the Canadian economy down to the level of disaster. They suddenly tried to reverse the whole posture and appear as a government led by a Prime Minister advocating restraint.
Health Resources Fund Act
This not only shook up the whole country, but it shook up the cabinet as well, particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who indicated in a press conference at that time that he really did not know what was going on with respect to government policy. All of us who watched that press club interview over television had great sympathy for the Minister of Finance. He had been placed in an impossible position by the sudden change in direction of the Prime Minister. It is not the first change in direction, as Charles Lynch stated in a recent column. It is the tenth manifestation of the Prime Minister of Canada. We do not know what the position is going to be from one moment to the next.
It is obvious the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) was placed in the same position of uncertainty, not knowing the direction the Prime Minister was charting, or if he even knew the direction he was charting. She was immediately faced with severe cutbacks on policies which the hon. member for Ottawa West referred to with some degree of positive appreciation this afternoon. We agree with that. However, suddenly there is a cutback which faces the provinces that are very dependent on the federal government for leadership, both in terms of its over-all approach to health and welfare and also for the financial basis of health and welfare programs.
Here are some of the cuts: $55 million in equalization grants, $150 million by deferring the community services program, $160 million by deferring the social services legislation. I want to pause there for a moment. For six or seven years we have been promised that there would be a major breakthrough in health and welfare programs with the introduction of the long-anticipated social services legislation. It began with a five-year review which produced the orange paper under the leadership of a former minister of national health and welfare who is now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde). Seven years later, we are still being given nothing but hope and promises with regard to this legislation. But let me continue with the recital of the cutbacks. They include $25 million under the public utilities income tax transfer, making a total of $390 million and the bill presently before the House would increase that amount by $29.5 million, bringing it up to $420 million. One can understand that the Minister of National Health and Welfare who assumed the portfolio a little over a year ago was faced with an impossible situation. As my hon. friend from Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) said in his speech last evening, she was obliged to take a scatter gun approach in trying to cope with it.
I have read her speeches with great care. She is obviously trying to put the best possible face on the situation, trying to give the government a humanitarian face, though that is an impossibility. I believe her heart is in the right place, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said; he believes the minister is trying to do her best in circumstances which have been created by the policies of her leader. She demonstrated this quality when she was faced with protests from the Indian community-I shall not dwell on that

It is incomprehensible that the government would attack the most vulnerable group with respect to health care by removing rights which are not only traditional but established by treaty. I should like to compliment the minister in another regard. All we are seeking is a committee to co-ordinate our activities in this field. That proposition has been repeatedly turned down, but I did receive a letter from the minister dated December 5 which indicates that she is wrestling with this problem and wishes to do something about it even though the social services legislation will not be in place in time for the 1980 World Congress on Rehabilitation. She says in her letter:
You can infer from these comments that a new motion along the line of your previous ones will receive my endorsation and support.
I appreciate that gesture of support and goodwill; it seems it should have been given long ago. We are now faced with the situation that our social services legislation will not be in place in time for Rehabilitation International, the worldwide community of people and organizations interested in rehabilitation which Canada is hosting in Winnipeg in 1980. I have been talking about the marvellous breakthrough which was on the horizon because we would be implementing the new legislation. So we shall get together a committee which will make it possible for representatives of the voluntary sector of the rehabilitation movement in this country to clarify their plans. There are at least 48 separate organizations led by the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled which are making preparations for this great congress. Six thousand people from around the world will be meeting in Winnipeg and we shall be able to hear from those representatives of the voluntary sector; we shall be able to get it all together and make a report on the state of rehabilitation in Canada which will be available as background information.

subsubtopic: DISPLAY OF THE FLAGS OF CANADA IN PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-220, respecting the presence of the flags of Canada in both Houses of parliament, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise to propose and explain the provisions of Bill C-220, which would provide for the display in the House of Commons and the Senate of the other Canadian flag, the Union Jack.
To the uninitiated my bill might seem a reactionary proposal; the placing of a symbol of the British Empire within the precincts of a building which the BBC has called Britain's first, but not last, export of fairyland parliamentary gothic.
But seriously, hon. members should realize two facts: first, the Parliament of Canada, after approving the Maple Leaf flag in December of 1964 immediately designated the Union Jack as another legal and legitimate Canadian flag; and second, the legitimacy of that flag is enforced by its special role as a reminder of our loyalty to the Crown and of our membership in the Commonwealth of nations.
I would like to examine these aspects of the symbolism of the Union Jack with a view to analysing why it should be displayed in this chamber.
To begin with, the Union Jack reminds us of our loyalty to the Crown. Indeed, Canada has always been a monarchy in an unbroken line. From the day that Jacques Cartier planted the fleur-de-lis of the Bourbon kings on the soil of New France in 1534 we have been a royal people whether under French, British or, since 1867 and more particularly 1831, a Canadian monarch.
In 1867 Canadians deliberately and freely chose the monarchy as their system of government. They could have adopted any other form of administration, but they chose, as do their descendents today, deliberately and specifically to maintain a constitutional monarchy, reflective of Canada's heritage dominant in Canada's present, and essential to Canada's future.
In chorus, unbroken from the earliest days, Canadian leaders, citizens and various constitutional conferences of more recent times have methodically decided that Canada should continue to be a sovereign state of which the Queen is head.
Indeed, one might add parenthetically that the monarchy even antedates the arrival of French colonists, for it, in a rather absolute variety, was the form of government known to Indian tribes in the millennium before the white man ever set foot upon this continent.
Of course, the constitutional monarchy is more democratic than a republic, for the Queen of Canada represents all Canadians. A president or other elected head of state would be a divisive factor in our land, as he would owe his selection to some political faction or other. This could divide him from
Flags of Canada
many of his countrymen and make his claim to represent all Canadians less convincing. This danger is inherent in the kind of muddled thinking which obtains in some quarters these days where it is fashionable to suggest that the monarchy and the person of the sovereign are mere ceremonial trappings and where these revisionists would claim the full amplitude of Canadian government is represented in the office of governor. However, now is not the time to enter that debate, but to reflect that the Queen and her heirs have been trained from birth for one profession and therefore by the most ultimate form of democracy-the chance arrangement of genes-they have become the Canadians most eligible to assume their important position.
It is worth noting that the most stable of democracies in the world today, our constitutional monarchy, is in direct contrast to the unstable tyrannies which are so often typified by a republican form of government. Indeed, we have a twentieth century monarchy for, through modern communication devices, Canadians can participate fully in their Queen's life wherever she may be, and she herself, when allowed, is able to visit and is aware of more parts of Canada than most Canadians.
Then, of course, newcomers to Canada today can either identify with the monarchy because they come from countries which enjoy that form of government or feel a special affection for their new sovereign because she typifies unity, rule of law and decency, which have all too often been absent in the countries from which they have fled.
The colour and ceremony surrounding our monarchy attracts the interest of all Canadians, especially the young, in our process of government. No less an ardent French Canadian nationalist than Henri Bourassa referred more than once to "the Crown we have come to respect".
The monarchy, despite its detractors' efforts to paint a contrary picture, is popular in French Canada. Historically, Francophone Canadians have three times chosen the monarchy. Their cultural and religious leaders rejected the overtures to join the rebellious colonists during the American revolution in 1776. They participated enthusiastically in the choice of the monarchy as the new state's form of government in 1867 and continued to accept it, as evidenced by the strong support given to the maintainance of the monarchical system by Premier Levesque and his minister of intergovernmental affairs, Claude Morin, at recent federal-provincial conferences.
Our Queen is a fluent speaker of the French language, and the early history of her house is closely bound with that of the French crown and French culture. Moreover, the Crown has always been an emblem of the guarantee that the rights of any minority will not be trampled by the will of a majority.
Now, continuing to reflect on why the flag most closely associated in Canada with the Crown and our Queen should stand in this chamber, let us remember that the Queen is the bond joining each Canadian to each of his fellow citizens.

February 2, 1979
Flags of Canada
When a new Canadian swears his oath of allegiance, he makes a personal contract to bear true and faithful allegiance to his sovereign. Thus, the immigrant acquires a lifelong tie in common with all other Canadians.
That the Queen is part of parliament, despite the best efforts of some, reflected in Bill C-60, to remove her; that she gives royal assent to legislation; that laws are enacted in her name and bear the year of her reign; that she provides the framework for orderly transaction to elected governmental officers; that the army, the mails and the civil service function in her name: these are not the accidents of history. These are not the curiosities of legal draftsmanship. They stand at the centre of the Canadian constitution, safeguards of Her Majesty's right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn and to provide practically the only check on the untrammelled growth of the power of the political executive.
In 1973, speaking in Toronto, Her Majesty said:
I want the Crown to be seen as a symbol of national sovereignty belonging to all. It is not only a link between Commonwealth nations, but between Canadian citizens of every national origin and ancestry. The Crown is an idea more than a person, and I want the Crown in Canada to represent everything that is best and most admired in the Canadian ideal. I will continue to do my best to make it so during my lifetime, and I hope you will all continue to give me your help in this task.
No one can argue that Her Majesty has kept and continues to keep this pledge, although how much help she has had from some of her ministers in the interim is at the very least debatable.
Thus, as we sit here in this chamber day by day and are looked upon not only by the thousands of young Canadians, especially who sit in the gallery and see our deliberations, but also by the new-found audience of millions brought to us here through television, I ask: is it not well that the flag standing for our affection and duty to Our Sovereign Lady and to the Crown she personifies should be displayed next to Your Honour's chair, a boast of that affection freely given and perhaps the departure point for many questions which will be asked by young Canadians about the significance of that flag, the answers to which will increase their knowledge of our country's institutions?
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we should not forget the second stated purpose of parliament to retain the Union Jack as a flag of Canada, namely, to stand for our membership in the Commonwealth, that unique association of sovereign states with vastly differing populations, traditions and systems of government, which, nonetheless, forms one of the few, if not the only, non-governmentally allied international communities on this shrinking planet.
I do not need to remind hon. members of the many contacts, exchanges and programs which enrich both our own experience and those of other Canadians through the various associations which promote international relationships. But, in that the centre of the Commonwealth is an allegiance to the Crown, and in that Canada is the most senior member of that body, again I ask: is it not well that the flag standing for that

shared allegiance and multinational association stand here in this chamber again to provoke questions for the uninitiated and to remind the more tutored of our international dimensions?

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Daudlin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
subsubtopic: DISPLAY OF THE FLAGS OF CANADA IN PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in this debate with a feeling almost of deja vu in that although I was not in this place at the time the great flag debate took place, certainly I was one of those concerned Canadians who listened with interest to what was said here.
Before I get into that aspect of the debate, I think it would be unwise of me to leave unchallenged some of the references made by the hon. member who preceded me to Bill C-60 and particularly the claim he makes that members of this government, or indeed any member of the House, would attempt by that bill to denigrate in any way royalty, the Crown, the Queen or anything having to do with the royal family.
Members of this government and members on this side of the House both in and outside the House have taken the position and have attempted to make clear-and obviously have not made it clear enough for the hon. member to understand-that the words used in Bill C-60 are not intended or designed to remove any of the rights or the authority of the Crown. What they are attempting to do is to delineate, underscore or describe, if you will, the status quo and what in fact is the current position of the Crown and the monarchy in Canada. I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said this in words more eloquent than I can repeat this afternoon, but if those words are not sufficient to describe what is the state of things, then let those persons who feel they do not provide those words that would describe the current state of the Crown, and again I say, not the Crown of 1900 or the Crown of 1867, but the monarchy as it exists today. Surely that is what was intended by the bill and that is what continues to be the intention of the government, as I understand it.
The debate today in a sense almost transports us back to 1964 when the House debated the flag. It was emotional, it was lengthy, and covered the merits of adopting a distinctive flag for Canada, a flag that would reflect our identity as a nation. It was a worthy debate. Those few members who were present in the House at that time may well recall the arguments which took place then. However, the majority of us, as I indicated earlier, were in other places, occupied with other concerns, and although we may have followed the debate with some interest, I think it might be enlightening and useful in the discussion of this bill to outline some of the history behind our national flag and the reasons why parliament in 1964 adopted the practices that surround its display in the House of Commons and in the Senate.
It is hard for us to imagine the emotion and strong feelings that were reflected in the debates at that time. By now, most Canadians have accepted the red maple leaf flag as the symbol of our aspirations, our ambitions, our legitimate national pride, our unity, our loyalty, our Canadian nationality. In spite of the many reservations expressed in 1964, I think that the majority of Canadians have developed an attachment for that flag and
February 2, 1979

what it stands for. In fact, the word "attachment" may even be understanding the case, because many Canadians have developed a respect, and some a love, for the flag that would be very gratifying to those in the government, especially the late prime minister, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, who was instrumental in introducing it before the House.
But such pride and acceptance were by no means assured back in 1964. There were many who were strongly attached to the great union flag, more commonly known as the Union Jack, and there were others equally partisan in favour of the Red Ensign, which for many years has served as the de facto Canadian flag. These supporters were difficult to convince of the need for a unique and distinctive Canadian flag, and they mounted a vigorous opposition which at several points threatened to delay and perhaps scuttle the government's plans to introduce the single red maple leaf flag so familiar to us today.
In the present context, when we are being asked to consider the introduction of the Royal Union flag within the chambers of the House of Commons and the Senate, I think we should review and reflect upon the decision of the House in 1964 to limit the Union Jack to be used as a symbol of Canada's membership in the Commonwealth of nations and of her allegiance to the Crown. This decision was not taken lightly or without a great deal of reflection. In giving primacy to the national flag, and in limiting the use of the Union Jack to certain occasions, such as the official observance of the Queen's birthday, the anniversary of the Statute of Westminster, and the occasion of royal visits and certain Commonwealth gatherings, the House was making a strong and deliberate statement on the subject of Canadian identity.
Much thought had been given to the ideal design for a Canadian flag. The committee of the House that was formed to choose a suitable design reviewed hundreds of suggestions sent in by experts and by the public at large. Design after design was eliminated until only three were left. Some of you may recall them: there was a red and white design containing the Union Jack and three fleurs-de-lis, a design incorporating three maple leaves on a white background with a narrow bar of blue at either end, and the familiar red flag with a single red maple leaf on a central white square. As we all know, on October 22, 1964, the House voted unanimously in favour of the single leaf flag that has become so integral a part of our lives. It was officially proclaimed and flown for the first time on Parliament Hill on February 15, 1965-in the words of John Matheson, member of parliament for Leeds, Ontario, who had originally been charged with the responsibility for finding a new flag design, "a flag of dignity and grace, worthy of a great sovereign nation".
Speaking in 1979, it is difficult to project oneself back into the atmosphere of those pre-1964 days and to imagine a time when this nation lacked an official, central symbol of its own identity. Following confederation in 1867, the Union Jack of Britain was retained as the official flag of Canada. That was perhaps appropriate at the time because Canada was still a colony of Great Britain and not a full-fledged nation. Our first prime minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, reacting to the first
Flags of Canada
stirrings of Canadian nationalism, requested formal approval from the British Admiralty in 1874 to use the Red Ensign, bearing the provincial arms of the four provinces then in confederation, as the official Canadian flag. This approval was denied until 1892, and even then it was granted only on the condition that its use be confined to Canadian merchant ships on the high seas. Nevertheless, it is interesting to note that Canadians continued to fly the Red Ensign, on land as well as on sea, until the outbreak of the Boer War, when a resurgence of imperial feeling throughout the British Empire revived popular support for the Union Jack, and the Red Ensign was removed from all Canadian public buildings. Therefore, during the First World War Canadians fought and died under the Union Jack. For all intents and purposes they were considered to be British troops, in spite of the fact that most of their regimental badges contained such distinctively Canadian symbols as the maple leaf and the beaver, and that Canadians distinguised themselves in their valorous stands at such battlefields as Vimy Ridge and Ypres.
After the First World War, Canadian nationalism once again became a strong force, and King George V was persuaded, on the recommendation of the government of Sir Arthur Meighen, to grant a Canadian Coat of Arms in 1921. This was incorporated quickly into the Red Ensign, and in 1924 the Canadian government authorized the use of the Ensign on all Canadian buildings outside Canada. Canadians were left in the very peculiar position of being able to fly the Red Ensign outside but not inside their country. Even after the passing of the Statute of Westminster in 1931 when Canada became a fully autonomous nation, the Union Jack remained the official flag. There were numerous attempts by members of parliament during the 1930s to introduce flag motions in the House.
During the Second World War, a distinctive battle flag was designed by the Department of National Defence for use by Canadian troops. It was not a popular success. Many people, and indeed members of the House who were familiar with the military, cannot indicate the design of that flag. In 1943 a return was made to the Red Ensign which was authorized to be flown by the Canadian army formations overseas. After the war the then prime minister, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, announced that he would recommend to parliament the adoption of a distinctive national flag. In the meantime, a 1945 order in council was passed which indicated that until a national flag was adopted, the Red Ensign would be flown over federal buildings both inside and outside the country. This temporary expedient proved to be a much more enduring one than even Mackenzie King would have envisaged. The new flag design placed before parliament in 1946 was rejected on the grounds that it might not be acceptable to all Canadians. In spite of periodic attempts to revive the flag issue, the nation remained in a state of limbo, in so far as the flag was concerned, until 1964 and the events I have already described.
I do not mean to abuse the patience of the House by giving this lengthy history of our attempts to adopt a truly Canadian flag. Instead, I think it is a necessary background to discus-

February 2, 1979
Flags of Canada
sions of this bill. For years as a nation we were without one of the central symbols of nationhood. During that time we struggled to identify who we were as a people. As we slowly severed the links of colonial status we gradually came to an understanding that our flag, whatever it might be, could not be a copy or a derivative of any other nation's flag. It would have to be distinctly our own, using symbols which were unmistakably Canadian and embedded in our history.
The final choice admirably fulfils this requirement. In heraldic terms it is described as "gules in red on a Canadian pale argent of white a maple leaf of the first". The maple leaf, the central feature of the flag, is perhaps the quintessential Canadian symbol. As early as 1700 it was already in use in Canada. In 1834 it was adopted by the Saint-Jean-Baptiste society as its emblem. By 1860, when the Prince of Wales visited Canada, citizens of Toronto unanimously approved a motion resolving the following:
All native Canadians joining in the procession, whether identified with the national societies or not, should wear the maple leaf as the emblem of the land of their birth.
As I mentioned before, the dominant symbol of Canadian regimental badges as early as the First World War was the maple leaf. Finally this fact was recognized officially in the Coat of Arms of Canada, which in its original form had three green maple leaves on a single stem and a golden lion holding a red maple leaf above the shield. Later in 1957 the colour of the three maple leaves on the coat of arms was changed from green to red, to correspond with Canada's national colours.
Also the colours of red and white were incorporated into our flag. They strengthen the symbolic significance of the design; the red represents strength and the white purity. But beyond these two admirable qualities, they form a part of the tradition of both France and England, our two mother countries. Red was the colour of St. George's Cross and the colour borne by the French crusaders. White was the colour of the field of St. George's Cross and the colour of the banners borne by Joan of Arc. For a long time white was the colour associated with the early monarchs of France, just as red was the colour of the early kings of England. In his proclamation of the Canadian Coat of Arms in 1921, King George V officially recognized red and white as the Canadian colours. Thus, it was fitting they should form part of our flag.
Having taken 98 years to develop and agree upon this emblem of our country, it is not difficult to understand why our predecessors in the House were reluctant to authorize the equal recognition of another flag within the Canadian context. The debates of 1964 were enlightening. Many members who participated in the weeks of debate preceding the adoption of the flag were singularly unenthusiastic about the motion to adopt the Union Jack as the Commonwealth flag. This was not because hon. members lacked respect for the Union Jack and for what it stood. Many were strong supporters of the Commonwealth and the monarchy; many opposed the superseding of the traditional Union Jack and Red Ensign by any new flag. However, once the red maple leaf flag had become fact, they understood the need to stand behind their decision. There

could be no half measures and no recognition of two flags, especially two flags which stood for such different realities. Those members realized that to be a successful embodiment of this country, the flag would have to command the undivided allegiance of its citizens; it would have to be clear indication of Canada's sovereignty and nationhood; and its meaning could not be diluted by legislation which made provision for the recognition of another flag, except in the most unusual circumstances.
The amendment finally adopted limited official display of the Union Jack to those occasions I have outlined already: the Queen's birthday, royal visits, Commonwealth gatherings, the anniversary of the Statute of Westminster, and at war memorials during ceremonies marking anniversaries of events in which Canadian forces participated with other Commonwealth forces. Even on those occasions, the Canadian flag must be flown and must be given the precedence due the national flag. Of course individuals and organizations were allowed to continue to fly the historic Un;on Jack when appropriate, as long as they took into consideration the form of approval accorded it by parliament. Our predecessors wished to ensure the primacy of the new flag. In the light of subsequent events, very clearly they succeeded.
During the debates several members expressed their fears that Canada was adopting a "two flag" system which would lead ultimately to divisiveness and strife. They saw, some more clearly than others, that the national flag could become a unifying force if it were given a chance, or a source of dissent if it were not.
Looking at the Canadian flag from today's perspective, I think they adopted the correct course. There may be many sources of disunity in this country today, but I do not think the flag is one. The flag flies proudly on all our public buildings; school children wave thousands of tiny versions of it during public holidays and royal visits. It is even a popular form of window curtain among the younger generation, a use which may not be officially sanctioned but nevertheless is an index of acceptance. One of our most moving national moments occurs each July 1 when a giant Canadian flag is raised on the Peace Tower as the culminating moment of a day-long celebration.
Such widespread approbation is no accident. It is a direct result of the actions taken by the House 15 years ago. We were correct to adopt our flag then and to make it the undisputed symbol of our national consciousness. We will be correct now to oppose this bill which proposes that we take a step backward and dilute the authority we have invested in our flag. I urge the members of this House to consider carefully the long struggle toward true nationhood which preceded the adoption of our flag. I urge them to reflect upon its current stature and undisputed place in the hearts of Canadians. I hope they will conclude that in the chambers of this House, of all places, it should remain the sole and undisputed symbol of our collective identity.

member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Daudlin) take a position in his concluding comments. I hope the hon. member has not mistaken the intent of this legislation. We in no way want to downgrade the importance of our Canadian flag, the red maple leaf of which the majority of us are very proud.
I should like to support recognition for the Union Jack in both Houses of parliament. As the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) said, the Union Jack was recognized by an act of parliament of 1964 as one of Canada's national flags and it has played an important role in the history of our country. It signifies our place, and recognition of the role we play in the Commonwealth. For that reason I would be most happy to see it in both chambers of parliament.
I cannot help but be somewhat suspicious when hon. members opposite speak on issues associated with the monarchy. So often we see them use the monarchy for purposes of political expediency. In this chamber and throughout the country they have tried to diminish the role of the monarch in the Canadian way of life, yet when we have visits from the royal family the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is front and centre, trying to gain whatever political points he can.
As I said at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, my comments will be brief in the hope that this bill will come to a vote within the hour allotted for private members' business so that we can see where hon. members stand on issues associated with the Union Jack and with the monarchy in general.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on the subject before us, namely the Union Jack.

I can well imagine that when this debate was going on in this House some 15 years ago, tempers were a little sharper than they are today. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) was here at that time and took part in the debate. I would have welcomed the chance to put my views forward at that time as well.
I noticed earlier this afternoon that the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was in the House, Mr. Speaker. I had hoped that he would take part in the debate.
The hon. member who spoke ahead of me said that he was glad my colleague the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Daudlin) stated his position. I state my position categorically, Mr. Speaker. 1 am opposed to the Union Jack standing side by side with the Canadian flag in this chamber or in the other place. I am as opposed to that as I would be to having the tri-coulour of France if it were brought forward to take its place there.
The hon. member opposite said that our roots are deep in the traditions of England and British history. I do not deny that. Indeed, I am glad of it. This parliament stands today as a
Flags of Canada
model of what was accomplished in terms of parliamentary democracy in England. I would be the last person to make a derogatory statement about the great traditions handed down to us by England. But this was in another time, Mr. Speaker. We should remember our roots but we should also look to what we are in the present and what we hope to aspire to in the future.

Mr. Speaker, symbols have that remarkable characteristic of combining various and often complex notions in a vivifying and colourful expression. The symbolism of the Canadian flag we are talking about here reflects the history, the beliefs, the ideologies and the aspirations of Canadians who are multicultural and who today, with the passage of the Official Languages Act, are known throughout Canada. In addition, proclaimed on February 15, 1965, the maple leaf became the distinctive, sober and gracious symbol of this country, as the former hon. member for Leeds, Mr. Matheson, put it so well.
Indeed, on February 15, 1965, on Parliament Hill, in Ottawa, the ceremony of inauguration of the Canadian flag took place in the presence of the right hon. Georges Vanier, Governor General of Canada, Prime Minister Lester B. Pearson and the members of the cabinet. These words spoken on that memorable date by the hon. Maurice Bourget help emphasize the symbolic aspect of our flag which is on your right, Mr. Speaker. He said:
This flag is the symbol of the unity of this country because it represents beyond the shadow of a doubt all citizens of Canada without distinction of race, language, belief or opinion.
In 1964 the Parliament of Canada after adopting the maple leaf as the flag of Canada proclaimed the Union Jack as the official symbol of the belonging of this country to the Commonwealth. I want to describe the use made of those two flags to further emphasize the importance of our Canadian flag.
When physical facilities permit, the Union Jack flies with the Canadian flag on buildings, air terminals, military bases and establishments of the federal government within Canada on the day of the official celebration of the Queen's birthday, the anniversary of the Statute of Westminster, which is December 11, as you know, and during royal visits and certain Commonwealth meetings in this country. It can also fly with the Canadian flag at the national monument commemorating the dead of World War I and in other appropriate public places in Canada during ceremonies commemorating the anniversary of events in which Canadian and other Commonwealth forces participated. Of course, individuals and organizations can fly the Union Jack in Canada as they see fit under the regulations approved by parliament for the use of the flag.
On the other hand, the Canadian flag is, of course, flown in more places and on more occasions that the Union Jack. In general, we can see the Canadian flag from sunrise to sunset flying over all federal buildings, airports and military bases and institutions inside and outside Canada. Regulations also

allow it to be flown all night. It can also be used in commercial buildings or to identify Canadian stands at exhibitions. It constitutes the normal national colours of all Canadian ships and boats, including pleasure craft. In fact, the Canada Shipping Act provides that a Canadian ship must fly the flag on a signal given by one of Her Majesty's ships or a ship on the service of the Canadian government and belonging to the government, while entering or leaving any foreign port, and if it carries a burden of 50 gross tons or more, while entering or leaving any Commonwealth port.
Foreign vessels fly the Canadian flag as a sign of courtesy when they lie at anchor in a Canadian port. In the case of merchant vessels and pleasure craft, the Canadian flag must be flown in all ports and in territorial waters. However, this rule does not apply on the high sea unless the vessel wishes to show its nationality to another ship. When a merchant vessel and a warship, whatever their nationality, cross or pass each other, the merchant vessel must salute with its flag as a show of courtesy.
Mr. Speaker, the flag is used, of course, at the unveiling of monuments, plaques and paintings, at the end of conferences or official inaugurations, on national holidays, and so on. It is also used to note the death of important personalities or officials. Thus, the flag on the Peace Tower in Ottawa is flown at half mast on the death of the sovereign or a member of the royal family, on the death of a governor general, a former governor general, a lieutenant governor, a member of the Canadian Privy Council, a senator or a federal member of parliament.
Besides being flown on top of other buildings, airports government military establishments and federal government buildings, the flag will be flown at half mast from one end of the country to the other on the death of a sovereign, a member of the royal family, the governor general, the prime minister, retired governors general, retired prime ministers or ministers of the federal cabinet. Secondly, within the confines of the provinces, the flag will be flown at half mast on the death of a lieutenant governor, the first minister of the province or any person to whom the province wishes to pay respect. Thirdly, the flag can be flown at half mast on the death of a member of a provincial legislature in his or her riding and, fourthly, the place of residence in the case of the death of a senator, a past member of the Privy Council of Canada or a mayor. [Translation]
The flag is also flown at half mast on federal buildings and elsewhere according to special instructions on the death of members of the royal family other than the sovereign or of persons related in the first degree with the sovereign and his immediate family, as well as on the death of a foreign head of state or any other person whom we may wish to honour.


Such was the case after the death of President Kennedy of the United States when he was assassinated some 16 years ago.

During half-mast periods, the flag is flown to the top of the mast on all federal buildings, airports and military bases and establishments during all legal holidays, and on the Peace Tower when a chief of state visits Parliament Hill. However, that rule does not apply when flags are mid-masted on the occasion of the sovereign's death, they are hoisted to the top of the mast only the day the new monarch is proclaimed.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, on November 11, Remembrance Day, the flag on the parliament building's Peace Tower is mid-masted at 11 a.m.
In light of all those examples, hon. members will agree that our Canadian flag is significantly utilized. Even when the Queen is in Canada, Her Majesty's own Canadian flag is hoisted,

She has her own royal flag, and it is not the Union Jack because that is the flag of Britain. The royal flag varies from country to country within the Commonwealth, and the royal flag is flown in these countries when the Queen visits. [Translation]
Let me go on, Mr. Speaker, day and night the Queen's flag, a unique flag, is proudly hoisted on any building where she is residing or in which she is attending an official or public reception. Generally, the colours also fly behind the tribune where Her Majesty is saluted by the troops she is reviewing, and on Her Majesty's ships when she is aboard.
I therefore feel, as a large number of my electors, that the Canadian flag is the symbol par excellence of our Canadian identity.

I therefore ask myself why we should adopt the Union Jack to stand beside our own flag. Even though it does symbolize our membership in the Commonwealth, it is not the responsibility of Canada alone to determine which flag should be used to signify association with the Commonwealth, but a decision which should be taken together with all other member nations of the Commonwealth.

Of course, we have no suggestion whatsoever to Commonwealth countries wishing to use the Union Jack as their own flag. Anyway, I sincerely believe we can show our participation in the British Commonwealth by using our own flag, because it adequately reflects our cultural identity.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I oppose for these reasons the Royal Union flag being present alongside the national flag in the Senate and House of Commons.

The hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Daudlin) mentioned that those men and women who fought in the first and second world wars did, indeed, use as their flag the Union Jack. As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs i represented Canada at Vimy last November 11 and was taken on a tour of the cemeteries where our Canadian brothers and sisters of another time lay buried. Engraved on their headstones in a circle was the maple leaf, the same maple leaf which we have on our flag. It took 98 years before we could call this flag our own and before we could fly it on this building. As a fifth generation Canadian, I make no apology for saying that no other flag should stand beside ours. This flag was bought and paid for by all the other Canadians which make up this great country, and, as the hon. member for Kent-Essex has said, we would be taking a step backward if we did not proclaim once and for all that this is the flag of Canada and of all Canadians. It is my flag and I am very proud of it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the debate that has taken place and to all the members who have made a contribution. It is their right in private members' hour to express their opinions. I will try not to use up all of the time so that my friend on the other side can express his opinion as well. I disagree with the hon. member for Kent Essex (Mr. Daudlin) but only on two matters, as he gave an admirable recount of the history of the time. I disagree with him that Bill C-60 did not appear, to a large number of people in the community, to do something in respect of the monarchy. In my opinion that was evident by the reaction in the community. People can think for themselves, they do not need members of parliament to tell them how to think in that sense.
I do not know if it was a conscious attempt or not, but at least it was perceived as such and as a result the government quite rightly backed down on what they intended. Right across the country the government said they did not intend that kind of thing, and it was even mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. This was all to the good because it was best for the air to be cleared.
The hon. member for Kent-Essex said that this debate takes us back to the flag debate. It may do so in the minds of some, but it should not. The flag debate was a watershed in the development of national symbols in this country. That flag was accepted by parliament, not without difficulty, but it was accepted. It seems to me that the red maple leaf flag has been generally accepted across Canada as a symbol of the nation. One can ask my children and children of other hon. members who were young at that time what is the Canadian flag. There is no doubt in the world that these children can tell you what flag is the Canadian flag. Indeed there is no doubt at all about what members of parliament feel when they distribute these small lapel pins to school children and others who come to visit this building. They are distributing a replica of the national
Flags of Canada
flag. There is no doubt that we have moved past that period of history and so I disagree with the hon. member for Kent-Essex in that regard.
When I look at Bill C-220 I see two things in the explanatory note. First I see that the Maple Leaf flag was proclaimed as the national flag and it says:
-the Union Jack as the symbol of our connection with the Commonwealth and loyalty to the monarchy.
This is a national parliament and a national chamber. As a private member of this House I think the only flag that should be in the national parliament and in this chamber should be the national flag. But that is not to say there is any movement away from those symbols which are important to me and many Canadians regarding our connection to the monarchy. This is a connection which has now been embraced by the government, according to the proclamations that we have heard.
We look around us and see the mace on the table with a replica of the Crown on it. There is a coat of arms on the chair. On top of the calendar on the table there is a Crown. On the ancient ink-well on the table is a Crown. A great deal of symbolism can be found in this chamber which indicates our affection and loyalty to the Crown.
With respect to the flag which is the national symbol of our country, I do not think it is inappropriate that it stands by itself as a national symbol. Symbols are important to people and that is the reason why I make these remarks. I do not want anyone in this House on either side to think that the Union Jack with all its traditions and with its three crosses is not important to a large number of Canadians and not part of the symbolism of the country.
If one looks at provincial flags, for example, the provincial flag of Newfoundland, the newest partner in confederation, he will see it happens to be the Union Jack. I am sure if one would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), a senior member of parliament in that area, how he feels about that flag he will find that he feels a sense of affection and identifies that flag with his lovely province. One can see the Union Jack on the Ontario provincial flag. I think that is quite appropriate. Indeed, the Union Jack appears in the fly of another provincial flag. I am sure the government leader in the Senate and the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) would be distressed if one ever said to them that the Union Jack contained in their British Columbia provincial flag was not important to them. It is an important symbol to many people. It is an important symbol to me, just as I am sure that symbol in those flags is important to others in this chamber who come from various provinces.
I do not believe this bill moves in the right direction. I know what the hon. member has in mind. I think there is a place for display within this building for the flags and the symbols which are important for the men and women who come to this building to serve in the House of Commons and the Senate from all provinces and from our two territories of this country. It would be appropriate if all members of parliament during the course of this debate gave some thought to a place within
